paragraphs: Our Sages said: a person should always be careful with the Minchah prayer, for Eliyahu (of blessed memory) was answered specifically through the Minchah prayer. One must be careful not to say it without a minyan and repetition (chazarah) except in a time of genuine need and unavoidable necessity, and one should clasp the two hands together, the right hand over the left, close the eyes, and pray.

clarification.explanation: The Sages said that a person should always be careful with the Minchah prayer, for the prophet Eliyahu was answered specifically through the Minchah prayer. One must be careful not to pray it alone — that is, without a minyan and the chazan's repetition — except in a time of genuine need and true unavoidable necessity, where there is no other option; and one should clasp the two hands together (right over left), close the eyes, and pray.
takeaways: One must take special care with the Minchah prayer (on account of the precedent of the prophet Eliyahu).
It is preferable to pray Minchah with a minyan and the chazan's repetition, rather than alone — praying alone is only for a time of pressing need and true unavoidable necessity.
Custom: clasping the hands (right over left) and closing the eyes during the prayer.

paragraphs: Although it is found explicitly in Sha'ar HaKavanot that our teacher the Ari (of blessed memory) was careful to pray Minchah only close to sunset, as our Sages said on the verse "They shall fear You as long as the sun endures" (Tehillim 72:5) — he had a special minyan that would pray with him and would wait until that time arrived, and there was no concern of being held up; but every person must be prompt with a mitzvah, for if one waits until that time, it is possible that business matters will come up and the time will pass and he will not pray.

clarification.explanation: Although it is recorded that the Ari would pray Minchah only close to sunset, this was because he had a special minyan that waited together with him, and there was no concern of being held up by other matters; but an ordinary person must be prompt with the mitzvah — lest matters come up for him if he waits, and the time of prayer pass.
takeaways: One should not wait to pray Minchah until close to sunset (that is only for one who has a special arrangement) — one should be prompt and pray earlier.

paragraphs: The Minchah prayer was instituted corresponding to the afternoon Tamid offering, and the time for the afternoon Tamid begins at six and a half hours, that is, half an hour after midday. However, the Tamid was not actually offered at this time — six and a half hours — except on the eve of Pesach that falls on a Friday, when they needed to attend to the Pesach offering before Shabbat entered, since its roasting does not override Shabbat, and they were compelled to slaughter the Pesach offering after the Tamid and not before; therefore on that day they would bring the Tamid forward, slaughtering it right at the beginning of its time as given by the Torah, which is half an hour after midday. But on the other days of the year they would not offer the Tamid except at nine and a half hours; therefore, optimally (lechatchilah), one should not pray Minchah before nine and a half hours, and this is called in the language of our Sages "Minchah Ketanah" (the small Minchah). After the fact (bedi'avad), if one prayed from six and a half hours he has fulfilled his obligation, since there was indeed a Tamid offered from six and a half hours on the eve of Pesach that falls on Friday, and this is called in the language of our Sages "Minchah Gedolah" (the great Minchah). Even so, although we have said one should not optimally pray Minchah Gedolah, nevertheless in a time of pressing need — such as one who wants to set out on a journey, or has a great matter of business, and is concerned that he may become preoccupied and forget and the time of prayer will pass — then it is permitted optimally to pray Minchah Gedolah, which is from six and a half hours. And the same law applies on the holy Shabbat, for one who wants to go hear the sermon from the preacher, who prolongs the sermon, and if he prays after the sermon he will not have leisure to make the third meal (Se'udah Shelishit) comfortably — it is permitted for him to pray Minchah Gedolah.

clarification.explanation: The Minchah prayer was instituted corresponding to the afternoon Tamid offering, whose time begins at six and a half hours (half an hour after midday). In practice, the Tamid was offered at this time only on the eve of Pesach that falls on a Friday (in order to have time to slaughter the Pesach offering before Shabbat entered); on the rest of the days of the year it was offered at nine and a half hours. Therefore, optimally, one prays "Minchah Ketanah" (from nine and a half hours), and after the fact — or in a time of pressing need (setting out on a journey, an urgent matter, or on Shabbat when waiting for a long sermon) — it is permitted to pray "Minchah Gedolah" (from six and a half hours).
takeaways: Optimally, one prays "Minchah Ketanah" (from 9:30 seasonal hours).
In a time of pressing need (travel, an urgent matter, a long sermon on Shabbat) — "Minchah Gedolah" (from 6:30) is permitted.

paragraphs: These hours of six and a half or nine and a half are called "seasonal hours" (sha'ot zemaniyot), because they are measured according to the length of the day, whether it is long or short, dividing the day into twelve parts. And wherever our Sages measured in hours, they measured in these seasonal hours; some say one measures from dawn (amud hashachar) until the stars come out (tzeit hakochavim), and some say from sunrise until sunset. The first opinion is the primary one, since we are stringent to measure from dawn until the stars come out, and this is likewise the plain custom here in our city of Baghdad, may it be built and established, to measure from dawn until the stars come out — for among us, the emergence of the stars is reckoned as a third of an hour after the calling of the maghrib in this city, and so it was received to measure this matter from the crown of my head, the great Rabbi, my grandfather, our teacher Rabbi Moshe Chaim, of blessed sacred memory.

clarification.explanation: These hours (six and a half or nine and a half) are called "seasonal hours," since they are measured according to the length of the day — the day is divided into twelve parts. And wherever our Sages measured in hours, one measures in these seasonal hours; and there is a dispute: some say one measures from dawn until the stars come out, and some say from sunrise until sunset; and the first opinion is primary, being stringent to measure from dawn until the stars come out, and so too is the plain custom in Baghdad — there they reckon the emergence of the stars as a third of an hour after the calling of the muezzin (maghrib) in the city, and so it was received to measure this from his grandfather's teacher, Rabbi Moshe Chaim, of blessed memory.
takeaways: "Seasonal hours" = dividing the day into twelve parts according to its length.
There is a dispute whether one measures from dawn until the stars come out, or from sunrise until sunset; the primary opinion (and the custom in Baghdad) is from dawn until the stars come out.

paragraphs: One must be careful to pay a hired worker's wages on the same day, before the Minchah prayer. And Rabbi Chaim Vital (of blessed memory) wrote that our teacher the Ari (of blessed memory) was very careful about this: if he did not have money in hand to pay, he would delay praying the Minchah prayer until sunset in order to seek money to pay the hired worker, and he would take a loan and pay, and only afterward would he pray the Minchah prayer in haste, for he would say: "How can I pray to the blessed Name when a great mitzvah such as this has come into my hands and I have not fulfilled it?" — see there. Therefore, every person should be careful and prompt in this matter.

clarification.explanation: One must be careful to pay a hired worker's wages on the same day, before the Minchah prayer. The Ari was very careful about this: if he did not have money in hand to pay, he would delay praying Minchah until sunset in order to seek money, and would even take out a loan in order to pay, and only then pray in haste — because he did not want to come to prayer while such a great mitzvah remained unfulfilled.
takeaways: One should pay a hired worker's wages before the Minchah prayer (following the example of the Ari, who even borrowed money in order to pay on time).

paragraphs: Although in the Minchah prayer the giving of charity is not obligatory as it is in Shacharit, nevertheless our teacher the Ari (of blessed memory) was accustomed to give charity also at Minchah before praying, and he would give three perutot in the manner that I wrote regarding Shacharit (Vayigash, 13), namely that he would give into the hand of the gabbai or the second poor person coins together, and afterward the third one, in the secret of two-thirds and a third, as mentioned regarding the charity given during the recitation of "Baruch she'amar" of Vayevarech David, as mentioned above — all of this is explained in Sha'ar HaKavanot, page 76, column 3, see there — and so it is fitting for every person to do. And fortunate is the man who is careful to pray Minchah wearing tefillin, called "Shimusha Rabba," which our teacher the Ari (of blessed memory) was always careful about. And I have already written above in the laws of tefillin (Vayera, 23) that the crown of my father's head, my father, of blessed sacred memory, was careful to pray Minchah during the month of Elul and the Days of Awe wearing the tefillin of Shimusha Rabba — may he be remembered for good in this world and the World to Come. And one who follows this practice should be careful not to remain wrapped in tallit and tefillin after sunset, as is explained in Sefer HaKavanot, that our teacher the Ari (of blessed memory) was very concerned about this matter. And it is a great mitzvah to be among the first ten men (asarah rishonim) also at Minchah.

clarification.explanation: Although at the Minchah prayer giving charity is not obligatory as it is at Shacharit, the Ari was accustomed to give charity before Minchah as well — three perutot (two together, and a third separately, in the secret of "two-thirds and a third"). And it is fitting for every person to do so as well. It is also fitting to pray Minchah wearing tefillin ("Shimusha Rabba"), as was the custom of the Ari and of Rabbi Yosef Chaim's own father, provided one does not remain wrapped in tallit and tefillin after sunset. It is a great mitzvah to be among the first ten men for the Minchah minyan as well.
takeaways: One gives charity (three perutot in the secret of two-thirds and a third) before Minchah as well.
It is fitting to be among the first ten men for the Minchah minyan, and not to remain in tefillin after sunset.

paragraphs: The time for Minchah extends until nightfall according to the Sages, but according to Rabbi Yehudah until "plag haMinchah" (the midpoint of Minchah), which is until eleven hours less a quarter, that is, an hour and a quarter before the stars come out. The law was not decided in accordance with either of them, and it was concluded that whoever acts like this one has acted properly, and whoever acts like that one has acted properly — meaning that one must always act consistently in accordance with one of them: if one acted like the Sages and prayed Minchah after plag haMinchah, he can no longer pray Ma'ariv before nightfall in accordance with Rabbi Yehudah, who holds that it is permitted to pray Ma'ariv after plag haMinchah. All of this is according to the law of the Gemara, but nowadays the practice has become lenient, and people follow two leniencies that contradict one another, praying Minchah and Ma'ariv together after plag haMinchah, and they have grounds to rely upon. However, this leniency was practiced only in public (with a congregation), but an individual praying at home cannot follow two contradictory leniencies: if he prayed Minchah after plag haMinchah, he may not pray Ma'ariv until the stars come out. And on the eve of Shabbat, when an individual wishes to pray Ma'ariv before nightfall, he should pray Minchah earlier, before plag haMinchah; but on other days he should not do so — rather it is better for him to pray Ma'ariv at night optimally, even though this means praying Minchah before plag haMinchah, because it is the choicest fulfillment of the mitzvah to pray Ma'ariv certainly at night, according to all opinions.

And I wrote in my small book Makabtziel that regarding a woman, one is not strict with her against making these two leniencies in this matter, since she is occupied with household affairs, this is considered for her a time of pressing need like the law of the congregation mentioned, and she may pray Minchah and Ma'ariv together after plag haMinchah as it happens to be convenient for her. And likewise regarding a man who prays alone at home and prayed Minchah after plag haMinchah: if he waits until definite nightfall for the Ma'ariv prayer he will certainly fall asleep together with the people who come [to join him], or there are other reasons — he may pray Ma'ariv after seven minutes have passed from the calling of the maghrib, which is called here in our city at the end of the twelfth hour.

clarification.explanation: The time for Minchah extends until nightfall according to the Sages, and according to Rabbi Yehudah only until "plag haMinchah" (an hour and a quarter before the stars come out). The law: each person should act consistently according to one opinion — if one prayed Minchah after plag haMinchah (following the Sages), he cannot pray Ma'ariv before nightfall (following Rabbi Yehudah). In practice, the public came to be lenient and combine both leniencies (praying Minchah and Ma'ariv close together, right after plag haMinchah), but this is only for the congregation; an individual praying at home should not do so — unless he wants to pray Ma'ariv early (such as on Friday), in which case he should also bring Minchah forward, before plag haMinchah. However, for a woman one is not strict about this: since she is constantly occupied with household affairs, this is considered for her a time of pressing need, like the law of the congregation — therefore she is permitted to pray Minchah and Ma'ariv together after plag haMinchah, whenever it happens to be convenient for her. Likewise, an individual man praying at home who already prayed Minchah after plag haMinchah — if he is concerned that waiting until definite nightfall to pray Ma'ariv will cause him to fall asleep (as happens when waiting together with others who are arriving), or he has some other reason preventing him from waiting — he may pray Ma'ariv already seven minutes after the calling of the maghrib.
takeaways: The congregation is accustomed to be lenient and combine Minchah and Ma'ariv close to plag haMinchah; an individual praying at home should not — unless he also brings Minchah forward.
For a woman, who is occupied with household affairs, it is always permitted to combine Minchah and Ma'ariv after plag haMinchah, as with the law of the congregation.
An individual man who is concerned about falling asleep (or has another reason) if he waits until nightfall may pray Ma'ariv already 7 minutes after the calling of the maghrib.

paragraphs: The calculation of plag haMinchah for praying Ma'ariv within it is done, according to the custom here in our city of Baghdad, may it be built and established, by reckoning from dawn until the stars come out, and our custom is to reckon the emergence of the stars as a third of an hour after the calling of the maghrib, which is called at the very end of the twelfth hour. And so the calculation goes: Minchah Ketanah is two and a half hours before nightfall, and half of this time is an hour and a quarter before the stars come out, since the time of their emergence is a third of an hour after the calling of the maghrib as mentioned. And if the day is twelve hours, that is, from dawn, then the time for the Ma'ariv prayer is at eleven hours and five minutes: how so — from the time of plag haMinchah, which is an hour and a quarter as mentioned above, subtract the third of an hour that there is from the calling of the maghrib until the stars come out, leaving the measure of plag haMinchah as one hour less five minutes; therefore we have said that once it becomes eleven hours and five minutes, one should pray Ma'ariv. And if the day is long, such that dawn is at the beginning of the tenth hour, so that the hours of the day come to fifteen, then these three extra hours are divided over the twelve hours, and each of the twelve hours becomes an hour and a quarter, and it follows accordingly that the hour and a quarter of plag haMinchah measures an hour and a half and four minutes, since by the reckoning of this day each quarter-hour measures nineteen minutes; subtract from this measure of an hour and a half and four minutes mentioned the third of an hour that there is from the calling of the maghrib until the stars come out, leaving this measure of plag haMinchah as one hour and fourteen minutes, so the time for the Ma'ariv prayer is at eleven hours less fourteen minutes. And if the day is short, ten hours from dawn, then the hours of this day are reckoned each at fifty minutes, and accordingly a quarter-hour is twelve and a half minutes, so the hour and a quarter of plag haMinchah is a measure of one hour and two and a half minutes; subtract from this the third of an hour that there is from the calling of the maghrib until the stars come out, leaving the measure of plag haMinchah entirely as forty-two and a half minutes, so it comes out that the Ma'ariv prayer is from eleven hours and seventeen and a half minutes.

clarification.explanation: The custom in Baghdad is to reckon the hours of the day from dawn until the stars come out, with the emergence of the stars fixed as a third of an hour (twenty minutes) after the calling of the maghrib (the call of sunset). The hours of the day are always divided into 12 equal "seasonal hours" (each seasonal hour = the length of the day divided by 12), and accordingly one calculates the time of "Minchah Ketanah" (two and a half seasonal hours before nightfall) and "plag haMinchah" — half of this time, that is, an hour and a quarter (seasonal) before nightfall — which is the earliest time to pray Ma'ariv. To get the time on an ordinary clock, one subtracts from the seasonal hour and a quarter the fixed third of an hour (the 20 minutes) between the calling of the maghrib and the emergence of the stars. The result depends on the length of the day: on an "ordinary" day of 12 hours (from dawn until the stars come out), the earliest time for the Ma'ariv prayer comes out at 11 hours and 5 minutes on the local clock — a clock whose end-point is the calling of the maghrib, that is, 55 minutes before that call; on a long (summer) day with 15 hours from dawn until the stars come out (and each seasonal hour longer, an hour and a quarter of an ordinary hour), the time comes out earlier — at 11 hours less 14 minutes; and on a short (winter) day with only 10 hours from dawn until the stars come out (and each seasonal hour shorter, about fifty minutes), the time comes out later — at 11 hours and 17 and a half minutes. That is: the longer the day, the longer its "seasonal" hours, and so plag haMinchah (in ordinary clock time) falls relatively earlier before nightfall; and the shorter the day, the shorter the seasonal hours, and plag haMinchah falls relatively later.
takeaways: The method: divide the day (from dawn until the stars come out) into 12 equal seasonal hours; plag haMinchah = an hour and a quarter (seasonal) before nightfall, minus the fixed third of an hour between sunset and the emergence of the stars.
On an ordinary day (12 hours): the earliest time for the Ma'ariv prayer is 55 minutes before the calling of the maghrib (11:05 on the local clock, whose end-point is the call).
On a long summer day (15 hours): the time is earlier — 74 minutes before the calling of the maghrib (10:46 on the local clock).
On a short winter day (10 hours): the time is later — 42 and a half minutes before the calling of the maghrib (11:17:30 on the local clock).

paragraphs: Until when may one pray Minchah? Behold, it is known that even according to the opinion of those who permit it under pressing need, one should not pray after bein hashemashot (twilight), and it is known that the measure of bein hashemashot is three-quarters of a mil, which is thirteen and a half minutes — see Shulchan Aruch, siman 261. And here in our city of Baghdad, may it be built and established, the early authorities examined and tested and saw that at a high place in the city, sunset is visible seven minutes before the calling of the maghrib; therefore I concluded in my holy book Rav Pe'alim, in a responsum, with the help of Heaven, that here in our city one may not pray Minchah except until six minutes after the calling of the maghrib, for until six minutes it is called bein hashemashot and one may pray Minchah within it in a time of pressing need, according to the opinion of those who permit it. And if so, one should not begin praying except until four minutes after the calling of the maghrib, so that the majority of the Minchah prayer will fall within bein hashemashot. And there are places where sunset is, for them, ten minutes before the calling of the maghrib, as the great Rabbi Chaim Palagi (of blessed memory) wrote regarding one city, and they should measure the time of bein hashemashot according to what is found in their city. And I have heard that the custom of the holy city of Jerusalem and Hebron, may they be rebuilt and established, is that once the maghrib has already been called, one does not pray Minchah at all, neither on a weekday nor on Shabbat, and this is according to the testimony of the Gaon the Chida (of blessed memory) — see Machazik Berachah, siman 261, letter 7, and siman 454, letter 2, and see further in Birkei Yosef and Machazik Berachah, siman 331, and Aderet Eliyahu, siman 13, and Tiferet Adam, siman 11, and Lev Chaim, siman 134, see there.

clarification.explanation: Until when can one pray Minchah? Even according to the lenient opinion — not after "bein hashemashot" (twilight), whose measure is three-quarters of a mil (about 13.5 minutes). In Baghdad it was examined that sunset appears seven minutes before the calling of the maghrib (the muezzin's call), and therefore it was determined that Minchah is permitted under pressing need only until six minutes after the calling of the maghrib (and one should not begin praying except until four minutes after it, so that the majority of the Minchah prayer falls within bein hashemashot). And places where sunset differs by a different measure from the call should measure bein hashemashot according to what is found in their city. In other places (such as Jerusalem and Hebron) the custom is to be more stringent — not to pray Minchah at all after the calling of the maghrib.
takeaways: In Baghdad: Minchah is permitted under pressing need until six minutes after the calling of the maghrib — and one should not begin except until four minutes after it, so that most of the prayer falls within bein hashemashot; and elsewhere one should measure according to what is found in one's own city.
In Jerusalem and Hebron the custom is stricter: not at all after the calling of the maghrib.

paragraphs: Regarding the Minchah prayer: if one began the verse "My Lord, open my lips" but had not yet begun the blessing, and heard Kaddish, Kedushah, or Barechu, I concluded in my holy book Makabtziel that he should answer the Kaddish and Kedushah, and then return to say the verse "My Lord, open my lips" and pray. And although in truth this verse is included within the Amidah prayer, it is not comparable to the law of the first "Yihyu leratzon imrei fi" (May the words of my mouth find favor) that I wrote about above (Beshalach, 22), which is included within the prayer, such that even though one heard Kaddish and Kedushah after the sealing of the blessing, he should not answer before the verse "Yihyu leratzon" — there it is different, because if he were to answer it would constitute an interruption in the middle of the prayer, for which there is no remedy; whereas here this is not the case, since there is no blessing with [God's] Name and Kingship in this verse, there is no interruption here, for he can go back and say it a second time. However, there I raised a doubt as to a case where one had already begun "Baruch atah Hashem" — whether he should finish "Lamdeni chukecha" and answer Kaddish and Kedushah, and afterward return and begin from "My Lord, open my lips" and pray; or whether we say that since he has already mentioned "Baruch atah Hashem" for the sake of a blessing, he is not permitted to make the mention for the sake of [completing] the verse, since they only said to do so [i.e., truncate to the verse] in a place of necessity, so that his blessing not be in vain — which would result in mentioning the Name of Heaven in vain. And this doubt has not yet been resolved for us.

clarification.explanation: One who began the verse "Hashem, open my lips" before the blessing of the Amidah, and heard Kaddish, Kedushah, or Barechu — should answer, and then return to say "Hashem, open my lips" and pray (unlike the first "Yihyu leratzon" that comes after the sealing of the blessings, where one should not answer beforehand — because that would be an interruption in the middle of the prayer with no remedy; here, since this verse contains no [Divine] Name and Kingship, one may repeat it). And one who had already begun and said "Baruch atah Hashem" — the Ben Ish Chai leaves it in doubt whether he should finish "Lamdeni chukecha" and then answer, and did not decide the matter.
takeaways: One who heard Kaddish/Kedushah/Barechu while still saying "Hashem, open my lips" and before beginning the blessing — answers, and then repeats the verse and prays; one who had already said "Baruch atah Hashem" — the matter remains in unresolved doubt.

paragraphs: Regarding a haircut: although Maran (of blessed memory) forbade it close to Minchah Gedolah, nevertheless there is room to be lenient where there are two or three additional pairs of scissors available by the barber, as mentioned in Magen Avraham, siman 232, se'if katan 3; and although there are those who differ and hold that the Sages did not distinguish [between cases], and see Eliyahu Rabbah — nevertheless there is room to rely on those who are lenient, and therefore people have become accustomed to permit this after Minchah Ketanah has arrived, and so is the plain custom here in our city of Baghdad; see also Eshel Avraham, siman 251, end of letter 5, see there. However, one who fears Heaven should be stringent about this, since in any case, according to the kabbalistic tradition, it is not proper to have a haircut after midday even if one has [already] prayed Minchah.

clarification.explanation: Although Maran forbade having a haircut close to Minchah Gedolah, there is room to be lenient when there are two or three additional pairs of scissors available at the barber (so that if one pair breaks in the middle of the haircut, one will not be delayed and lose the time for Minchah), and so was the custom in Baghdad — even after the time of "Minchah Ketanah" has arrived. Nevertheless, one who fears Heaven should be stringent, because according to the kabbalistic tradition it is not proper to have a haircut after midday even if one has already prayed Minchah.
takeaways: It is permitted to have a haircut close to Minchah if there are backup pairs of scissors available at the barber (the custom in Baghdad); one who fears Heaven should be stringent, according to the kabbalistic tradition, and not have a haircut after midday.

paragraphs: It is likewise forbidden to enter the bathhouse close to Minchah Gedolah, as Maran (of blessed memory) wrote; and here in our city there are those who enter even after the time of Minchah Ketanah, and no one protests against them, but in my opinion they have nothing to rely upon; therefore it is good that one take along to the bathhouse a person to watch over him, in order to remind him about the prayer, so as to fulfill the words of our Sages. It is likewise forbidden to judge a court case close to Minchah Gedolah, as Maran (of blessed memory) wrote, and here in our city the judges are not careful about this, and they have nothing to rely upon.

clarification.explanation: It is likewise forbidden to enter the bathhouse close to Minchah Gedolah, and although in Baghdad there are those who enter even after Minchah Ketanah without protest, in Rabbi Yosef Chaim's opinion they have nothing to rely upon — therefore it is good to bring along a person who will keep watch and remind one about the prayer. Likewise, it is forbidden for judges to adjudicate a case close to Minchah Gedolah, and in Baghdad the judges are not careful about this.
takeaways: Entering the bathhouse and adjudicating a court case are forbidden close to Minchah Gedolah; it is good to bring along a person who will remind one about the prayer.

paragraphs: Regarding a festive meal: here in our city they are lenient regarding a great feast such as a wedding or a circumcision and the like, and even after the time of Minchah Ketanah has arrived they are lenient regarding a great feast, and their basis is that among those reclining at the meal there are people who do not eat bread and also do not drink wine or beer at that meal, and only taste a little and eat a small amount of food, since that is not their main meal, for afterward they go home and eat; therefore these are considered like watchers who remind the other diners. And if everyone is eating and drinking, it is good that they appoint for themselves one watcher who does not eat and drink with them, so that he may remind them; and an individual eating at home, after the time of Minchah Ketanah has arrived, due to necessity and some cause, should appoint a watcher in order to fulfill the words of our Sages.

clarification.explanation: At great feasts (weddings, circumcisions) in Baghdad, they are lenient even after Minchah Ketanah has arrived, based on the fact that among the diners there are those who do not eat bread or drink wine/beer but only taste a little (and eat their actual meal at home afterward) — these serve as "reminding watchers" for the others. If everyone is actually eating and drinking, it is good that one watcher who does not eat sit with them, in order to remind them. Likewise, an individual eating at home after Minchah Ketanah due to necessity should appoint a watcher to remind him.
takeaways: At great feasts after the time of Minchah Ketanah, one relies on those who eat only a little to serve as "reminding watchers," or one appoints a dedicated watcher.
